name: Color analysis

card.summary: Seasonal colour analysis: matching clothing and makeup palettes to skin undertone, hair and eyes; popular and low-risk, but little rigorous research backs its specific categories.
card.aka: seasonal color analysis, color draping, 'finding your season'
card.note: Different analysts and apps can assign the same person to different seasons; published validation is sparse.

quick.overview:
Color analysis sorts people into palettes, traditionally the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter, based on skin undertone, hair and eye colour. Followers wear the colours assigned to their season in the belief that these make skin look clearer and the face more harmonious.

The method was popularised in the early 1980s and went viral again on TikTok in the early 2020s. Its categories are widely used but have little peer-reviewed validation.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners hold coloured fabric near the face, usually in daylight, and judge how it affects skin, eyes and overall contrast. Variants add dimensions such as undertone, lightness and chroma, expanding the four seasons to twelve or more sub-seasons.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk. Critics cited in encyclopedia coverage point to subjectivity, oversimplified categories, paid consultations and the encouragement of buying new clothes. Early systems were criticised for centring white clients.

lead: Color analysis, usually called seasonal color analysis, is a system that advises people which colours to wear based on features such as skin tone, hair and eye colour. People are typically assigned to one of four seasons, winter, summer, spring or autumn, with winters and summers described as having blue undertones and springs and autumns yellow ones [1].

The modern system was standardised by consultant Carole Jackson, whose 1980 book Color Me Beautiful was a bestseller, building on earlier work by figures including Johannes Itten [1][2]. It resurfaced in the early 2020s as a viral trend on TikTok [1]. In looksmaxxing and style communities it is treated as a low-cost way to improve appearance through clothing and makeup choices.

Published scientific support for the specific season categories is limited. Encyclopedia summaries note some research that people prefer clothing hues harmonising with their skin tone and that colours influence mood, while describing the practice as having few rigorous peer-reviewed studies behind its core claims [2].
infobox: Four seasons; extended systems of 12 to 16 sub-seasons
Draping fabric swatches near the face; online quizzes and apps

paras: Practitioners assess skin undertone (warm, cool or neutral), value (lightness or depth) and chroma (brightness or muting), together with hair and eye colour [2]. In the classic four-season model, winters suit rich saturated shades, summers softer muted tones, springs bright warm colours and autumns earthy hues [1].

The core technique is draping: fabric swatches are held near the face, ideally in daylight because artificial light can distort perception, to see how each colour affects skin and eyes [2]. Quick at-home variants described include comparing white fabrics or gold versus silver jewellery, and wrist-vein checks [2].

Swiss artist Johannes Itten linked colour preferences to seasonal archetypes while teaching at the Bauhaus in the 1920s [2]. Suzanne Caygill opened a San Francisco salon in 1945 matching palettes to clients' complexions [2]. Carole Jackson, building on Itten and others such as Belle Northrup and Harriet Tilden McJimsey, developed her system in the 1970s and published Color Me Beautiful in 1980; the Washington Post reported her company grossed 2.5 million dollars in 1982 [1].

In 2000 Kathryn Kalisz introduced the Sci\ART system, which expands the seasons into twelve palettes using Munsell's hue, value and chroma [2]. Since the 2010s, self-draping tutorials and palette quizzes on TikTok and Instagram have spread the practice, and AI-powered apps appeared in the 2020s [2].

Critics in the 1980s argued that colour restrictions were overstated, and later critics said the original book used dated language about gender, focused mainly on white people, and placed nearly all people of colour in the winter category [1]. Encyclopedia coverage describes the field as quasi-scientific, notes that different analysts can assign the same person to different seasons, and says four categories oversimplify the continuous variation in human pigmentation [2].

The same source reports that independent tests found different apps can place the same person in different seasons, and that AI classifiers reach roughly 70 to 80 percent accuracy on skin-tone classification while diverging from human judgments in some cases [2]. It also records ethical concerns about consumerism and costly consultations [2].
No studies found. No clinical trial has tested whether wearing a personally assigned seasonal palette changes perceived attractiveness.

timeline.event: Johannes Itten links colour preferences to seasonal archetypes at the Bauhaus.[2]
Suzanne Caygill opens a San Francisco colour salon.[2]
Carole Jackson publishes Color Me Beautiful, standardising the four-season system.[1][2]
Kathryn Kalisz introduces the 12-palette Sci\ART system.[2]
Viral TikTok revival, sub-season expansion and AI colour apps.[1][2]
